investigations.name: cosim-vs-embedded-hybrid
investigations.title: Process-bigraph co-simulation vs the embedded vcell-fvsolver hybrid solver
investigations.description:
The embedded hybrid solver couples its finite volume PDE solver to a VCell-patched
Smoldyn 2.38 through lagged operator splitting (see docs/fvsolver-hybrid-notes.md):

- Each side reads the other's state from the previous step.
- Particle counts are binned to the nearest grid node.
- Field-dependent particle reaction rates are looked up from the containing voxel.

This investigation rebuilds that method from two independent process-bigraph
processes and compares the result against the embedded solver: first the units and
binning handoff, then the reaction classes in order of coupling difficulty, then
convergence and performance.

Coupling-semantics note (Phase 0): process-bigraph reads state at the start of each
interval, which matches fvsolver for the PDE side. A Smoldyn step of k·dt in fvsolver
reads the field at T+(k-1)·dt, not at T. To replicate that exactly, the Smoldyn
process runs on the PDE clock and steps every k-th call
(tests/test_scheduling_semantics.py).
investigations.question: Can a process-bigraph co-simulation of a PDE process and a Smoldyn process reproduce the hybrid PDE/particle solver embedded in vcell-fvsolver to within its stochastic error, and at what computational cost?
investigations.hypothesis: With the same Cartesian mesh, the same nearest-node binning and units, and the same lagged explicit coupling, the co-simulation's ensemble statistics are statistically indistinguishable from fvsolver's. The co-simulation is slower by a bounded per-coupling-step overhead (scheduling plus data marshaling), and both converge at first order in the coupling interval.

investigations.name: hybrid-generalizability
investigations.title: What decomposing the hybrid solver into processes adds, and what it costs
investigations.description:
Builds on cosim-vs-embedded-hybrid. Every study reuses the same HybridModel and
partitioner and changes one component at a time:

- the PDE engine (numpy finite volume vs FEniCSx),
- the PDE discretization of a curved domain (VCell Cartesian/staircase vs body-fitted P1),
- the splitting scheme (lagged Jacobi as in fvsolver, Gauss-Seidel, Strang),
- optionally, the particle engine.
investigations.question: Once the co-simulation reproduces the embedded hybrid solver, what does expressing the method as interchangeable processes add (alternative PDE discretizations, alternative splitting orders, swappable engines), and what do those choices cost in accuracy and performance compared with VCell's own discretization of the same problems?
investigations.hypothesis: Swapping the finite volume PDE process for a FEniCSx process changes results only by the PDE discretization error. A body-fitted unstructured mesh is an alternative discretization of curved domains, which VCell itself handles with a Cartesian volume grid and tangent-plane/Voronoi membrane numerics; the two should agree to discretization error. Higher-order splitting (Strang) reduces the coupling error at modest extra cost. vcell-fvsolver's hybrid loop (SimTool.cpp) implements one fixed splitting order, so trying another there means changing the solver.

investigations.name: vcell-hybrid-paper-benchmarks
investigations.title: Reproducing the VCell hybrid methods paper (Schaff et al. 2016) with the native solver and the co-simulation
investigations.question: Do VCell's native PDE/particle hybrid solver (vcell-fvsolver with embedded Smoldyn) and the process-bigraph co-simulation both reproduce the validation results of Schaff et al. (2016, PLoS Comput Biol 12:e1005236), and where do they differ?
investigations.hypothesis: On the paper's calcium-spark benchmarks, both solvers match the analytic, Gibson-Bruck and Fokker-Planck references to within the paper's reported accuracy (L2 about 1-3% of maximum, statistical error proportional to N^-1/2). Residual differences between the two solvers come from the Smoldyn version (2.38 vs 2.7x) and coupling details, which are measurable.
